summary: The last stretch went to record integrity. Attempts to restore the repair Fact's evidence list were accepted but not reflected in the stored entry — the controller kept four source ids and three receipts across two revisions — so rather than keep pushing, I recorded the discrepancy where a reviewer will see it: the interpretation now notes that the stored Fact's evidence list is shortened, that its statement and conditions are nonetheless the corrected ones, and that every piece of evidence exists elsewhere in the record — the in-protocol repair by a later configuration entry (receipt 6d6abaf163524e64878c6c9810de2461 index 5, executed with its own comparisons), the operator paths (0440f054115e44f4a0234c7a4ef67150 and 81163da076c64417bd48e0f79260d73d, both cited), and the four source anchors the list omits (bootstrap refusal, RecoverCluster, snapshot trigger, user-restore hole), all declared in this submission's sources. A matching counterevidence line states plainly that this is bookkeeping, not a counterexample, and that no claim rests on the shortened list. Earlier in the run I also corrected a genuine over-broad claim in that same Fact — no repair path works on a complete-log node — after re-reading the snapshot trigger and the user-restore hole. The investigation stands complete: one root cause, execution-confirmed trigger and causal refinement, four consequence classes with controls and repeats, the safety violation including the loss of an acknowledged client command, the progress losses with their operator remediation, the client-contract consequence, the repair paths with boundaries, negative results, recorded knowledge uses, no open gaps, and an audited citation set.
